Developers constantly tweak these systems to handle edge cases, like reflective floors or uneven surfaces, which still confuse even high-end devices. In essence, your smartphone becomes a miniature surveyor, calculating geometry while you browse. Without this mechanic, AR shopping would remain a clunky gimmick rather than a reliable tool.

FACT_HOOK: In AR shopping, sometimes objects disappear to make the illusion believable.

Without occlusion, objects float unnaturally, breaking immersion. Modern apps calculate depth from sensors or cameras to determine overlap, constantly updating as you move. Some advanced systems even account for semi-transparent items like glass tables or curtains. Developers often refer to this as “layered reality,” where digital and physical spaces intersect convincingly. The technique is subtle, but it’s critical for AR shopping to feel real—users unconsciously notice inconsistencies, which can destroy trust. Occlusion algorithms turn AR from a fun gimmick into a credible shopping assistant.
